expected.rationale:
The nested `([a-zA-Z0-9]+)+` quantifier is the textbook catastrophic backtracking shape: input that fails the match near the end forces the engine to explore exponentially many partitions. finding.explanation: The nested quantifier `([a-zA-Z0-9]+)+` is a classic catastrophic-backtracking (ReDoS) pattern. For an input consisting of N alphanumeric characters followed by a non-matching character (e.g. `"a".repeat(30) + "!"`), the engine must explore 2^(N-1) ways to partition the alphanumeric run into groups before concluding the match fails. At N=30 that is ~536 million backtracking steps, causing a multi-second hang on a single call. Because this is a validator that is almost certainly invoked on user-supplied input, an attacker can trigger a denial-of-service by submitting a crafted string. The outer `+` is redundant (the inner `+` already matches one or more) and should be removed, yielding `^[a-zA-Z0-9]+@...`.

duplicates.explanation: The regex rejects many valid RFC 5322 email addresses. The local-part pattern `([a-zA-Z0-9]+)+` allows only bare alphanumeric characters, so common addresses with dots (`john.doe@example.com`), hyphens (`j.doe@example.com`), or underscores (`user_name@example.com`) are rejected. The domain pattern `[a-zA-Z0-9]+\.[a-zA-Z]+` permits exactly one label, one dot, and one TLD, so subdomains (`user@mail.example.com`) and hyphenated domains (`user@my-domain.com`) are also rejected. Any caller relying on this validator will silently treat valid users as having invalid email addresses.
